sub_units.name: Threads & Runnable Interface
sub_units.content: Threads in Java allow concurrent execution of two or more parts of a program. A thread can be created by extending the Thread class or implementing the Runnable interface. The Runnable interface is preferred as it allows the class to extend other classes. Key methods include start(), run(), sleep(), join(), and interrupt(). Understanding thread creation, execution, and the difference between extending Thread and implementing Runnable is fundamental to concurrent programming in Java.

sub_units.name: Thread Lifecycle
sub_units.content: A Java thread goes through several states during its lifecycle: New (created but not started), Runnable (ready to run or running), Blocked (waiting for a monitor lock), Waiting (waiting indefinitely for another thread), Timed Waiting (waiting for a specified time), and Terminated (completed execution). Understanding thread states, transitions between them, and how methods like start(), sleep(), wait(), notify(), and join() affect the lifecycle is essential for writing correct multi-threaded applications.

sub_units.name: Synchronization
sub_units.content: Synchronization in Java is a mechanism to control access to shared resources by multiple threads to prevent data inconsistency and race conditions. Java provides synchronized methods, synchronized blocks, and the volatile keyword for thread safety. The intrinsic lock (monitor) ensures that only one thread can execute a synchronized block at a time. Understanding deadlocks, starvation, the happens-before relationship, and using synchronization effectively is critical for building reliable concurrent applications.

sub_units.name: Executor Framework
sub_units.content: The Executor Framework in java.util.concurrent provides a higher-level abstraction for managing threads and thread pools. Key components include Executor, ExecutorService, and ScheduledExecutorService interfaces, along with the Executors factory class for creating thread pools (fixed, cached, single, scheduled). The framework also introduces Callable (returning results), Future (representing async computation results), and CompletableFuture (for composable async programming). The Executor Framework simplifies concurrent programming and improves resource management over manual thread creation.

sub_units.name: Lambda Expressions
sub_units.content: Lambda expressions, introduced in Java 8, provide a concise way to represent anonymous functions (functional interface implementations). The syntax is (parameters) -> expression or (parameters) -> { statements }. Lambdas enable functional programming in Java, reduce boilerplate code, and are widely used with the Collections API, Streams API, and event handling. They can access final or effectively final local variables from the enclosing scope. Understanding lambda syntax, type inference, and variable capture is essential for modern Java development.

sub_units.name: Functional Interfaces
sub_units.content: A functional interface in Java is an interface with exactly one abstract method, annotated with @FunctionalInterface. Java 8 introduced several built-in functional interfaces in the java.util.function package: Predicate (boolean test), Function (transformation), Consumer (action without return), Supplier (value provider), UnaryOperator, and BinaryOperator. Functional interfaces serve as the target type for lambda expressions and method references, forming the foundation of functional programming in Java.

sub_units.name: Streams API
sub_units.content: The Streams API, introduced in Java 8, provides a declarative way to process collections of data using functional-style operations. A stream represents a sequence of elements supporting sequential and parallel aggregate operations. Key operations include intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, distinct, flatMap) and terminal operations (collect, forEach, reduce, count, findFirst). Streams are lazy (intermediate operations are not executed until a terminal operation is invoked) and do not modify the underlying data source.

sub_units.name: Method References
sub_units.content: Method references in Java provide a shorthand notation for calling existing methods using lambda expressions. There are four types: static method references (ClassName::staticMethod), instance method references on a particular object (object::instanceMethod), instance method references on an arbitrary object (ClassName::instanceMethod), and constructor references (ClassName::new). Method references improve code readability and are commonly used with the Streams API and functional interfaces.

sub_units.name: Optional Class
sub_units.content: The Optional class, introduced in Java 8, is a container object used to represent the presence or absence of a value, providing a better alternative to null references. Key methods include of(), ofNullable(), isPresent(), isEmpty(), get(), orElse(), orElseGet(), orElseThrow(), map(), flatMap(), and filter(). Optional encourages explicit handling of missing values, reduces NullPointerExceptions, and promotes more readable and maintainable code when used appropriately in return types and stream operations.
